item.title: 5th EMPACT Hackathon leads to the detection of 51 potential victims
item.description: An international operation involving 40 experts and investigators from 20 countries has identified 51 potential victims of human trafficking, as well as five suspects. Held in Amsterdam from 23 to 25 September 2026, the fifth EMPACT Hackathon against the digital aspects of human trafficking brought together police officers, labour authorities and specialists in online investigations, supported by Europol and Eurojust.

item.title: 27 arrests and 248 potential victims identified in action week against labour exploitation
item.description: Europol, the European Labour Authority (ELA), and 34 participating countries today announced the results of an action week targeting human trafficking for labour exploitation. The operation, part of an EMPACT action led by Sweden, brought together police, border guards, labour and social security inspectorates, and tax authorities to crack down on exploitative practices in high-risk sectors such as agriculture, construction, cosmetic services, massage parlours, and hospitality.

item.title: Tech Firms Dismantle Botnet That Turned 1.3M TV Boxes Into Proxies
item.description: Google said today it worked with industry partners to dismantle a botnet made up of more than 1.3 million Android TV set-top boxes that ship with malicious software which secretly rents the user's Internet connection out to strangers and conducts advertising fraud. Experts involved in the takedown say the action is likely to sever the botnet's access to more than 10 million additional compromised systems, including other Internet of Things (IoT) products such as Android-based healthcare devices and karaoke machines.

item.title: Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: AL26-028 – Ongoing Help Desk Voice Phishing Campaign Targeting Canadian Organizations
What a security strategy that survives 2027 looks like
item.description:
Equifax CISO Jeremy Koppen sees the same dynamics most security chiefs are facing: hackers on the one side using AI to perform more sophisticated attacks at unprecedented speed, and defenders on the other adopting AI to match that volume and velocity.

“AI is changing the pace on both sides,” he says. “Attackers are using it to operate at greater scale, and Equifax is using it to innovate more quickly.”

In the next year, Koppen will continue to evolve Equifax’s security strategy to keep with an accelerating threat environment.

“That means building on the security already embedded across our design and development process, so checks run early and automatically,” he says. “It also means expanding how we use AI in our own security operations to handle routine work, so our experts can focus on the threats and initiatives that matter most. Done well, security becomes one of the reasons a product can launch sooner.”

As for the rising tide of AI agents entering enterprise workflows, Koppen says that “identity controls are central” to his 2027 security strategy.

“Across the industry, more activity on enterprise networks now comes from AI agents, bots, and automated workflows, and most traditional security controls were designed with a human user in mind,” he explains. “That’s why we’re applying the same rigorous verification to these identities that we apply to people.”

Of course, Koppen, like other seasoned security leaders, knows his IT security strategy must evolve to address more than just AI. Geopolitics, the anticipated arrival of quantum computing, and increasingly interconnected systems, are also changing the threat landscape and attack surface — sometimes in radical ways — and should prompt strategic changes, too.

That in turn is putting pressure on CISOs to rethink their practices, policies, and approaches as we head toward a new year likely to be at least as wild of a ride as 2026 has been.

“CISOs realize they need to transform, because their current state isn’t working. And it’s going to be a pretty significant transformation over the next few years for CISOs to be successful,” says Omar Khawaja, a CISO, a faculty member at Carnegie Mellon University’s CISO program, and a board member at HITRUST and FAIR Institute.

Of course, transformation, as always, is a work in progress, Khawaja says; as a result many security execs are still working out what needs to change in 2027 and how to make those changes happen.

Still, Khawaja, Koppen, and others stress that transformation is not an option; the safety of the organization depends on strategic evolution from its cybersecurity teams.

So what exactly needs to change? Security leaders point to specific elements that won’t work as well in the year ahead and what needs to be in place instead to more adequately secure the organization in 2027 and beyond.

Static credentials need to go

Koppen believes static credentials are on their way out.

“No matter how strict the policy, passwords still end up looking like a favorite sports team or the current season with an exclamation point at the end. That makes them trivial targets for brute-force attacks,” he says, noting that his company eliminated passwords across its 22,000 employees and contractors and is now extending its passwordless standard to its B2B customers.

More manual SOC work must be automated

The new command for security teams is to move at machine speed.

“We’re not able to deal with attacks and vulnerabilities manually anymore. AI is making that impossible,” says Florida State University CISO Bill Hunkapiller.

His security strategy reflects this new reality. He has been implementing autonomous agents to replace routine security operations tasks, and his 2027 plans call for expanding the number of tasks handled by machines.

Most CISOs are on this path. The State of Incident Response Readiness from Sygnia found that 32% of organizations have extensive AI use across most or all threat detection and incident response (IR) activities, up from 25% in 2025. And 63% expect to have extensive AI use in place for threat detection and IR activities in 2027.

Generic severity scores are out, risk ratings tailored to the organization are in

Equifax’s Koppen declares that generic severity scores are no longer effective. “A vendor’s ‘critical’ rating doesn’t know if a system holds sensitive data, is externally facing, or sits behind other controls,” he says, noting that Equifax has its own quantitative risk engine that factors in that context so its teams “can focus on issues that pose real risk to the business.”

Hunkapiller, who is also chief privacy officer and an adjunct professor at FSU, also sees a need to understand how common vulnerabilities and exposures pose a risk to his organization in particular, rather than relying on ratings. To that end, he’s exploring services that could create a digital twin of his environment to simulate how hackers could exploit vulnerabilities in his organization. This service would give Hunkapiller near-real-time information on which vulnerabilities pose the most significant risks to FSU, allowing him to accurately prioritize fixing those quickly, he says.

Thus far, he’s impressed with the capability, saying it’s like “attack surface management on steroids.”

Continuous patching is now the goal

Security used to have Patch Tuesday, a moniker that reflected the regularly scheduled work of applying newly released fixes to software flaws. Although security teams today may not adhere to Tuesday specifically for the work, many still patch on a set schedule — and many still take weeks to patch. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report puts the median time to remediate known exploited vulnerabilities at 43 days, up from 32 days in 2025.

That won’t fly in 2027, says Hugh Thompson, program chair for the RSA Conference.

“We used to do patching very methodically. If a patch came out for a system, we didn’t want to roll it out right away [for fear] it could break something. So we took time and tested it out and scheduled the work. That’s not going to work now, because the speed at which these AI attackers can take advantage of vulnerabilities or discover new ones is greater than ever,” he says. “We need automation in patching.”

Jason Rader, CISO for technology solutions and systems integrator Insight, has been accelerating his company’s patching program, bringing patch windows down to seven days for its most critical components — a significant accomplishment given the size of the IT environment and the number of patches being released. Still, he wants to do better, saying he’s aiming to increase speed for patching in all areas of the IT environment in 2027 and noting that he’d like to eventually get to continuous patching.

Different treatment for agent and NHIs needs to end

With AI agents doing more work that was, until recently, performed by humans, it’s becoming increasingly clear that security can’t treat machine identities — whether agents or systems or APIs — differently than humans, Rader says.

To that end, he’s already “managing agents like people,” applying equally diligent attention to managing identity and associated permissions — and, thus, access to data and systems — to ensure that each entity can access only what is appropriate for its role.

This includes managing machine identities throughout the lifecycle of those machines, just as security should for human workers, and applying proper governance, Rader adds.

Agility and adaptability must be part of the 2027 strategy

Some CISOs still take a set-and-forget approach to policies, procedures, and standards, says Prakash Venkata, a cyber, data, and tech risk partner at PWC and the firm’s security, risk, and engineering practice leader.

That approach never worked well, as there has always been a need to improve and evolve policies, procedures, and standards as the threat landscape and the attack surface changed, Venkata explains. But the pace of change now is so fast that CISOs need to build agility and adaptability into their strategies simply to keep up and meet industry standards.

Thompson likewise preaches the need for more agility in security strategies and advises security leaders to “be prepared for agility more than we had to or could stomach in the past because problems will emerge that you can’t anticipate.”

He notes, too, that CISOs need to work with other departments, such as procurement, to bring that needed agility to security. For example, if the CISO needs to quickly buy and implement new technology to reduce a recently identified risk or defend against an emerging threat, CISOs will need procurement procedures to move as fast as security must move.

Detached AI security and governance strategies become obsolete

There has been a rise of AI governance and security strategies that are detached from the organization’s overall governance and security strategy, says James Lyne, CEO of SANS, a security training and certification organization.

Lyne believes that the attention on AI governance and security is critical. However, he thinks having fully segregated AI governance and security strategies will be increasingly detrimental in 2027 and beyond. That’s because they’re not different and separate from enterprise governance and security.

“An AI app exposed to malicious inputs is an app security problem,” he says. “AI agents accessing unauthorized things is a privilege management and operation security issue [no less than] if people had unauthorized access.”

To ensure organizations have an effective, coordinated approach to governance and security capable of protecting the entire organization, where elements work together with no siloes or redundancies, CISOs and their organizations need a unified security strategy that addresses all actors — “whether they’re human, software services, or AI agents, or automated workflows,” he says.

item.title: Who approves the files that control your AI coding assistant?
item.description:
A pull request adds a helpful setup step for an AI coding assistant. No application source changes. The description calls it a developer-experience improvement, and the reviewer sees a short configuration file beside some Markdown instructions.

Before approving it, the reviewer needs to answer a different question: what will this change allow to run on a colleague’s machine?

The issue has moved beyond hypothetical repository poisoning. In an October 8 analysis of agent-skill distribution, StepSecurity revisited the June Miasma campaign, which planted AI-tool and editor configuration in a Microsoft repository without modifying application source. The configuration was intended to trigger credential harvesting through developer tooling. The October publication describes an inventory product, but the underlying campaign illustrates a wider operational problem: merging a configuration change can distribute execution instructions to the people working in that repository.

StepSecurity also reports that the commit carried a skip-CI flag and a backdated timestamp, and that it moved code execution from package install to folder open. A control that runs only in the build pipeline never sees that path. The first reliable checkpoint is the pull request, and it needs a person who knows what the file can trigger.

I recommend giving these changes a named owner and an enforceable review path. An organization should be able to identify who approved a hook, what the approval covered and where the approved version is allowed to run.

Review the behavior behind the filename

A repository file can serve several purposes. It may describe a coding convention, direct an agent toward a script, register a tool or arrange for a command to run at a lifecycle event. Those differences matter more than the extension.

A Markdown instruction is not automatically executable code. It can nevertheless influence an agent that has permission to execute commands. A JSON setting may directly register a shell command. Review should establish the mechanism, the trigger and the authority available when it fires.

Skills show why the filename is a poor guide. StepSecurity notes that a skill’s allowed-tools field can let the agent use listed tools without a permission prompt during the turn that invokes the skill, and that Claude Code’s documentation says workspace trust does not gate that field. A SKILL.md file is Markdown, so in a pull request it tends to be reviewed like a README.

Anthropic’s current hooks reference states that command hooks run with the user’s permissions. It also distinguishes interactive workspace trust from noninteractive operation: settings-file hooks in a repository can run in a noninteractive session without the trust dialog shown to an interactive user. The exact behavior depends on the configuration surface and session type. A control tested at a developer’s terminal should therefore be retested in the automated workflow that uses the same repository.

The same page names practical mitigations. Before scripting a noninteractive run over a repository nobody on the team wrote, review its .claude settings files, start the run in bare mode or turn hooks off for that run. Administrators can also use the managed-hooks-only setting so that user, project, local and plugin hooks are blocked. Which of these fits depends on the organization’s tooling, and each should be tested rather than assumed.

For a proposed setup hook, the reviewer should be able to trace the command to its script and dependencies. If the script downloads another program, determine how that program is selected and verified. If it reads credentials or accesses the network, ask why the setup step needs those capabilities.

These questions should accompany the change while its author can explain the intent. Discovering them after distribution leaves every affected developer to make an individual trust decision.

Make ownership enforceable

Engineering productivity teams are often best placed to maintain shared coding-assistant configuration. Security should define the conditions that require a second reviewer, such as adding executable hooks, broadening network access or invoking a new external tool. The application team remains responsible for whether the integration belongs in its workflow.

This need not create an approval queue for every formatting preference. Define the behavioral changes that warrant scrutiny and route those changes to people who understand the tooling.

GitHub’s code-owner documentation explains how ownership rules work with required reviews. A CODEOWNERS file alone does not make its approval mandatory; the corresponding branch protection must require it. GitHub also recommends protecting the ownership file itself.

Apply the chosen mechanism to the agent configuration and the scripts it invokes. Protecting a settings file while leaving its referenced helper script outside the review rule creates an obvious gap. Check the effective rule with a sample pull request rather than relying on the presence of a policy file.

Allow legitimate changes to move quickly through a known path. The reviewer should receive a concise explanation of the trigger, required access and expected side effects. A hook that formats changed files should not need the same justification as one that contacts an external service or modifies a user’s global configuration.

Check what the developer environment actually loads

Repository review covers only part of the environment. Developers can also install shared skills, plugins and user-level configuration outside a project. An approved repository may therefore run alongside additional instructions that its maintainers have never reviewed.

Establish a baseline for the supported tools and launch methods. Record the origins and versions of approved additions, and provide a way to inspect the effective configuration. When local copies differ, compare the content before deciding that the difference is malicious or harmless.

Microsoft’s Workspace Trust guidance for Visual Studio Code describes Restricted Mode, which limits features that can execute workspace content. It also warns that a malicious extension can ignore that boundary. Workspace trust is a useful control within its documented scope; it should be paired with a deliberate extension policy and an environment appropriate to the repository being inspected.

Use unfamiliar repositories in an isolated environment without routinely mounted production credentials. Avoid treating a container as sufficient isolation if it inherits the developer’s secrets or access to the host. Review those connections explicitly.

For approved daily work, make the safe setup practical. Publish maintained configurations, explain how to request an addition and provide a clean inspection workflow. If compliance requires developers to reconstruct their environment manually every morning, it will be difficult to sustain.

Test the approval path before trusting it

Run a benign exercise in a disposable repository and isolated environment. Add a hook that writes a harmless marker file. Check whether the pull request reaches the intended owner, whether an unapproved change can merge and whether the installed tool permits the marker action under the documented launch conditions.

Repeat the exercise through the noninteractive route if the organization uses one. Then change only the referenced helper script. That second change tests whether the review boundary covers behavior as well as configuration.

The result should identify which controls prevented execution and which merely recorded it. A scanner alert, required review and runtime restriction perform different jobs. Record the gaps without presenting one as a substitute for all the others.

Three questions make a workable first review. Who can merge a change to the files that steer our coding assistants? Does that rule also cover every script those files call? Which of our automated jobs run the assistant over code we did not write, and do they apply the same trust checks as a developer’s terminal?

For security leadership, the useful measure is whether changes capable of altering execution reach the right reviewer before distribution, and whether the working environment matches the approved scope. Start with one supported coding tool and one engineering team. Ask them to demonstrate who can change its behavior, how that change is approved and what happens when someone tries to bypass the process.

item.title: Cursor removes malicious Claude Code extension after SSH backdoor attempt
item.description:
A malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension distributed through the Cursor marketplace attempted to install a persistent Secure Shell (SSH) backdoor on developers’ machines, potentially giving attackers remote access to systems holding source code, credentials and other sensitive information.

“Between about 2:27am PT and 1:35pm PT today, a maliciously modified version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was made available in the Cursor VS Code Extension Marketplace,” Cursor said in a security notice.

Cursor removed the compromised versions, 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, after discovering they had been available in its VS Code extension marketplace for approximately 11 hours on October 29.

The company said the malicious code attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key, enable local SSH access, and establish a reverse tunnel to an attacker-controlled server.

“These malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic,” Cursor added in the notice. The affected versions were available for Windows and macOS.

Anthropic subsequently clarified how the tampered extension had been distributed. In a post on X, Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic’s technical staff, said the incident did not involve a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor had used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish the modified extension, he said.

“The versions on our official channels are not affected, and this only impacts Cursor users,” Rieseberg wrote. Anthropic said it was working with Cursor on the incident.

Cursor and Anthropic had not responded to requests for comment by publication time.

Malware ran without user interaction

Security company Phorion, which analysed the compromised extension, found that malicious code had been inserted at the beginning of its JavaScript file. It ran as soon as the extension loaded, before its normal activation code.

“The user doesn’t need to interact with the extension for the payload to fire,” Phorion said.

The malware attempted to add an attacker-controlled SSH key to the user’s authorized_keys file and establish a connection to a remote server. It also created scripts and startup entries intended to keep the connection available after a system restart, the company added.

Phorion identified a flaw in the macOS code. The malware tried to check whether Remote Login was disabled using a system command that required administrator privileges. When run without those privileges, the command returned an access error rather than the expected status. The malware consequently skipped the attempt to enable SSH.

Phorion also found an error in the Windows code that could prevent its SSH service setup command from running correctly.

Microsoft Threat Intelligence, in a separate analysis, detailed the information the malware collected, including machine names, usernames, operating systems, working directories, and Git email addresses.

“It also looks for environment-variable names containing terms such as KEY, TOKEN, SECRET, PASS, AWS, or GCP, keeping up to forty matches,” Microsoft wrote in the analysis. It said the code collected matching variable names, not their values.

Removing the extension may not be enough

Cursor said enabling the local SSH service would generally fail without administrator privileges on affected Windows and macOS machines. However, the extension could still add the attacker’s SSH key, install persistence mechanisms, and send host information to the attacker.

The company warned that uninstalling the extension alone might not remove these components because the malware placed scripts outside the extension’s installation directory.

Steve Povolny, vice president of AI strategy and security research at Exabeam, said the planted SSH key made cleanup particularly important. “Removing the extension only sends the visitor away while the spare key stays on the hook,” he said.

Povolny recommended checking authorised SSH keys on machines accessible to affected developers, rotating potentially exposed credentials, and reviewing logs for logins using unfamiliar keys. Developers often have access to source code, cloud accounts, and production systems, he said, making a compromised workstation a potential route to other enterprise resources.

Phorion also advised checking the SSH key’s fingerprint rather than relying only on the comment svc-telemetry attached to it.

Questions raised about extension security

Yash Kadakia, founder and CTO of Security Brigade, said enterprises should treat extension marketplaces as part of the software supply chain.

“An extension marketplace is effectively another software supply chain,” Kadakia said. “When malicious code can reach developers through what appears to be a legitimate, routine update, the traditional assumption that software from a trusted marketplace is safe starts to break down.”

He recommended stronger publisher verification, checks on package integrity, and controls over which extensions and versions developers can install.

Kadakia also called for extension allowlisting, controlled updates, endpoint monitoring, and restrictions on outbound connections. He said short-lived credentials, segregated development environments, and limited access to sensitive infrastructure could reduce the impact of a compromised developer machine. Cursor said it removed the malicious versions, temporarily shut down its marketplace, audited access, rotated keys, and rebuilt the marketplace before restoring the service.

item.title: Cyber chief: UK facing AI-powered attacks on critical infrastructure within two years
item.description: The NCSC warns that ‘tech on the cheap’ has left UK organisations exposed to AI uncovering and exploiting longstanding cyber security weaknesses and calls for urgent investment in resilience.

item.title: AL26-026 - Critical vulnerabilities impacting PHP - CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 - Update 2
AL26-027 - Critical vulnerability impacting Google Brotli – CVE-2026-111497
A compromised DevOps laptop caused the $6.3B Binance breach
item.description:
Cryptocurrency Exchange Binance blamed a compromised DevOps laptop for the loss of $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency last week, adding that it will now cover any losses faced by its customers.

“Binance will cover all losses from the Secure Assets Fund for Users (SAFU) and the company’s funds,” the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange said in an update on Friday, adding that user funds are safe and that it had found no evidence of wallet private-key leakage during its investigation of the incident. It had frozen approximately $3 billion in assets on-chain, temporarily suspending withdrawals while security checks were completed, and revoking the affected address authorization.

Withdrawals are now being restored in phases, initially reopening services across 15 networks, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, and XRP. Binance says it has replenished approximately 95% of the affected assets using company funds, while the remaining 5%, comprising less-liquid tokens, could take longer to source.

The exchange said its preliminary investigation pointed to a compromised employee device that enabled access to a service container involved in withdrawals.

“This attack, reportedly on a development engineer, highlights that security is a critical element of every operational stage and personnel level,” said Tim Rawlins, senior advisor and director of security at NCC Group. “When security failures in trusted identities and administrative access can be targeted, attackers can exploit more than just the underlying technical vulnerabilities.”

The FBI has since attributed the attack to North Korean threat actors, identifying the TraderTraitor hacking group as responsible for the theft.

“Given what we know about the activities of countries like North Korea in targeting cryptocurrency, it’s unsurprising that attackers are prepared to invest considerable efforts in targeting individuals who have access to the building blocks of the exchanges,” Rawlins said.

A compromised laptop reaches the withdrawal pipeline

Binance’s preliminary findings suggest that attackers compromised a DevOps engineer’s laptop before gaining access to a service container and submitting unauthorized withdrawals. The exchange has yet to publish technical details of the attack, leaving important questions about the precise intrusion path and how the attackers navigated its internal systems.

“A platform holding digital assets should have multiple layers of security to prevent a single compromise, such as an employee’s laptop being hacked, from being sufficient to authorize a transfer,” said Mario Rivas, blockchain and digital assets security lead at NCC Group.

The reported attack is similar to the February 2025 Bybit breach, in which attackers compromised a developer’s machine at Safe{Wallet} and manipulated the interface presented to transaction signers. However, the Binance incident involved a different mechanism.

F6’s Threat Intelligence Department (TID) said the Binance attack reportedly targeted an automated withdrawal process rather than directly deceiving authorized signers. Evgeniy Yanov, Head of Audit and Consulting Department at F6, cited Crypto security platform Blockaid, highlighting a batch of 50 EIP-7702 authorizations within a single transaction, alongside delegation to a malicious “sweeper” contract, as an unusual feature of the reported attack.

“This specific mechanism has not been seen before in large-scale breaches of this size,” Yanov said.

FBI points to North Korea’s TraderTraitor operation

The FBI has attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, an elite North Korean hacking unit considered part of the broader Lazarus infrastructure.

The agency, working with the US Secret Service and IRS Criminal Investigation, said it had observed the attackers converting stolen assets privately into Ethereum. It warned that the funds could subsequently be laundered through decentralized finance platforms and instant-swap services.

F6’s TID said the attribution was based on a combination of on-chain and off-chain intelligence. “The group’s signature matches previous thefts: small Tornado Cash withdrawals used to fund the operator’s wallet, extensive preparation well before the actual heist, and pre-signed transactions executed in a single burst,” it added.

TID researchers noted similarities with previous North Korean-linked cryptocurrency thefts, including the Bybit and KelpDAO incidents. However, they cautioned that Binance has not independently named the perpetrators and that the full attribution evidence has not been published.

Binance did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

NCC Group’s Rawlins noted that the growing use of AI could help attackers chain vulnerabilities and operational weaknesses together, while organizations increasingly face adversaries willing to invest considerable effort when the potential financial return is substantial. “Good cyber hygiene and effective security fundamentals are key to defending against attacks that many organizations are still missing,” he said.
